newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to talk tough with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to talk tough with Israel.

text.p: Jordan is likely to use the toughest language since its 1994 peace treaty with Israel when it tells the Jewish state this week that relations hinge on honouring peace accords, officials said on Sunday.

They said Jordan's ambassador to Israel Omar al-Rifai was to meet Netanyahu's political advisor Dore Gold on Sunday to arrange a higher level meeting this week with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to convey the "grave consequences" of Israel's tampering with peace accords.

"There has emerged not only lack of an Israeli desire to implement accords, but what is more dangerous than this is the Israeli call to open all files of past accords that have been signed with Arab parties, including Jordan," Information Minister Marwan Muasher was quoted as saying in Sunday papers.

Jordan is seriously questioning Netanyahu's willingness to honour past commitments -- citing failure to redeploy troops from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to fall under Palestinian self-rule in line with a 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal.
Officials are now underplaying the significance of what they say will be a ceremonial visit to Jordan expected sometime this week by Israeli President Ezer Weizman.

Instead they are focusing on a visit expected on Monday by Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to brief the king, due to arrive from London later on Sunday, on progress in resumed Israeli-Palestinians talks since a recent flareup in violence.
In recent days, King Hussein has stepped up his public support of Arafat while distancing himself from Netanyahu.

This represents a turnaround in his position. The monarch had urged wary Arabs to give Netanyahu a chance to show his intentions after his May election. This meant he was far more positive than other Arab leaders towards Netanyahu.
In a belligerent tone that has been absent in recent years officials now say that Israel's hardline policies are driving the region into a wider Arab-Israeli conflict.
Prime Minister Abdul Karim al-Kabariti was quoted as saying that "the situation in Palestinian territories had reached a point that threw all possibilities into the open."
Muasher said the present stalemate in the peace talks could only lead "to its collapse with only a sacred adherance to peace talks needed to avert it."
He said King Hussein, who warned Israel its policies could lead to war, was only "ringing the bells of alarm."
Officials say Jordan only went public in its criticism of Netanyahu after earlier pleas went unheard.

Worried officials say recent violence in Palestinian territories, which has left 75 dead, also raised the fear of chaos on the West Bank that could spill over into the kingdom because of close demographic, political and economic links.
